title: Hooke’s law and spring constant
prior_knowledge_summary: Tensile forces point away from an object’s centre and can produce extension.
Compressive forces point toward the centre and can shorten an object.
Extension is final length minus original length.
new_learning: State the condition built into Hooke’s law.
Use F = kx and k = F/x.
Interpret spring constant as force required per unit extension.
not_yet_taught: identification of the limit of proportionality from curved data

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct visuals support prediction, proportional scaling, symbol meaning, calculation, comparison and boundary checking.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Will twice the load always give twice the stretch?
content: Hang one small mass from a spring and mark its extension. Add an identical mass. A useful model predicts twice the extension, but only while the spring remains in its proportional region.
The puzzle is not whether a spring stretches. It is whether force and extension scale together, and when that rule stops being safe.

figure.brief: Three-panel spring sketch: unloaded, one load, two equal loads. Use matching extension brackets without drawing a full graph.
figure.alt_text: A spring with one load and two loads shows a proportional-extension prediction.

blocks.title: Hooke’s law includes a condition
blocks.accepted_definition: the extension of a material is proportional to the applied force, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded
content: The phrase provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded is part of the law. Leaving it out turns a conditional model into an unlimited claim.
Within that condition, doubling applied force doubles extension and halving force halves extension.

figure.purpose: Show proportional pairs without pre-teaching graph analysis
figure.brief: Use paired force-extension cards: 2 N to 4 mm, 4 N to 8 mm, 6 N to 12 mm, plus a boundary warning sign.
figure.alt_text: Paired values show force and extension increasing in the same ratio.

blocks.title: The formula to remember
content: Remember F = kx. F is applied force in newtons, x is extension in metres, and k is spring constant in newtons per metre.
Rearranging gives k = F/x and x = F/k. Use extension, not total length, for x.
The unit N m⁻¹ follows because k is force divided by extension.

figure.brief: Hand-drawn formula triangle or annotated equation with F, k and x linked to force arrow, spring label and extension bracket.
figure.alt_text: The equation F equals kx is annotated with force, spring constant and extension units.

blocks.title: Finding spring constant
content: A spring extends 15.0 mm when a force of 3.60 N is applied. Convert first: 15.0 mm = 0.0150 m.
Check independently: F = kx = 240 × 0.0150 = 3.60 N, so the rearrangement and unit conversion are consistent.

figure.brief: Annotated worked layout with 15.0 mm converted to 0.0150 m before substitution and a reverse check in a separate coloured box.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout converts millimetres to metres and calculates spring constant.

blocks.title: Using stiffness to predict extension
content: Two springs each carry 5.0 N. Spring A has k = 100 N m⁻¹ and spring B has k = 250 N m⁻¹.
A larger spring constant means more force is needed for each metre of extension, so the larger-k spring extends less under the same force. This is what stiffness means here.

figure.brief: Side-by-side springs under the same 5.0 N load with unequal extension brackets and k values labelled.
figure.alt_text: Two springs under equal force extend by different amounts because their spring constants differ.

blocks.title: The most common wrong substitution
content: It is tempting to put the spring’s final length into F = kx. The equation uses extension, which is the change in length.
If a 0.200 m spring becomes 0.212 m long, then x = 0.012 m, not 0.212 m. A quick size check should catch the mistake.

figure.brief: Before-and-after spring with original length, final length and only the difference bracket labelled x.
figure.alt_text: A spring’s total lengths are shown separately from its extension x.

blocks.title: A safe Hooke’s-law routine
content: Find extension in metres. Choose F = kx or a rearranged form. Substitute with units. Check whether the result matches the meaning of stiffness.
State the proportionality condition whenever the law itself is requested. Detailed recognition of where a real force-extension graph stops being proportional belongs to the next lesson.

concepts_taught: Hooke’s law as a conditional proportional model
spring constant as force per unit extension
misconceptions_addressed: using total length instead of extension
assuming a larger spring constant gives more extension for the same force
skills_students_can_now_use: calculate force, extension or spring constant
next_lesson_can_assume: F = kx within the proportional region
larger k means a stiffer spring
